This paper studies an important and timely problem: whether a black-box LLM API is actually serving the distribution users believe it is serving. The paper formalizes this as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, proposes MMD-based tests with string kernels, and empirically argues that a simple Hamming kernel is particularly effective in the low-sample regime. It then applies the method to commercial APIs serving Llama-family models and reports that a substantial fraction of endpoints appear distributionally different from Meta reference weights. Overall, I found the paper interesting, practically relevant, and likely to stimulate follow-up work. The framing is strong, the empirical question is consequential, and the paper’s main message is easy to understand: distributional auditing of LLM APIs is feasible with modest sample budgets.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation. “Model Equality Testing” is a clean abstraction that unifies several practically important auditing tasks: checking fidelity to open weights, detecting drift over time, and identifying model substitution. This is a useful contribution even independent of the specific test chosen. The paper also does a good job motivating why benchmark accuracy under greedy decoding is insufficient for many users, especially when the object of interest is the full sampled completion distribution on long-form tasks. That motivation is compelling and, in my view, one of the paper’s main strengths.

A second major strength is the empirical finding that a very simple kernel works well. The Hamming kernel over completions is computationally cheap, intuitive, and appears substantially more powerful than exact-match style tests in the small-sample regime. The comparisons against one-hot MMD and multinomial-style baselines are useful and support the claim that feature sharing across strings matters in high-dimensional output spaces. The experiments on quantization, watermarking, and finetuning are broad enough to make the central point believable. The API audit is also impactful: even if some individual endpoint conclusions may be sensitive to implementation details, the broader result that commercial endpoints can materially deviate from reference distributions is important.

That said, I have several concerns, mostly around statistical validity under realistic API conditions, the scope of the empirical evaluation, and interpretation of the audit results.

My main concern is that the paper’s statistical guarantees seem cleaner in the formal setup than in the actual API setting. The theory assumes the auditor has sample access to two distributions with the same prompt distribution, vocabulary, and decoding parameters. In practice, commercial APIs often differ in undocumented ways: tokenizer/version differences, hidden system prompts, safety filters, truncation behavior, stop-sequence handling, repetition penalties, top-p defaults, seed handling, and backend nondeterminism. The paper acknowledges some of this indirectly by moving to character space for cross-tokenizer comparisons, but the audit conclusions are still easy to over-interpret as “provider modified the model” rather than “provider endpoint induces a different observable completion distribution under our querying protocol.” The latter is still valuable, but the distinction matters. I would strongly encourage the authors to sharpen this throughout the paper, especially in the abstract and conclusions.

Relatedly, the choice to test equality of observable completion distributions means the method conflates many causes of deviation: model weight changes, quantization, decoding stack differences, prompt templating, safety interventions, caching, and even infrastructure bugs. That is acceptable if the claim is purely behavioral auditing, but some passages imply stronger attribution than the method supports. For example, statements about providers “serving different distributions than reference weights” are justified, but suggestions that this reveals quantization or substitution specifically are not, absent additional controls. The paper would benefit from a clearer taxonomy of what exactly is identified by the test and what is not.

A second concern is calibration and multiple testing in the API audit. The paper says tests are conducted at level alpha = 0.01 using N = 10m samples, repeated over ten samples, and endpoints “fail” if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5. This is not a standard hypothesis-testing procedure, and it is not obvious what overall false positive rate this induces at the endpoint level. Repeating a level-0.01 test ten times and thresholding the rejection proportion is a reasonable heuristic for variance reduction, but it changes the operating characteristics substantially. The paper should either provide a formal analysis or empirical calibration under null endpoints showing the effective endpoint-level Type I error. As written, the claim that the audit “flags 11 out of 31 endpoints” is hard to interpret statistically. This issue is especially important because the paper also tests multiple prompt distributions and multiple endpoints. The Bonferroni note in the figure caption is not enough; the main text should clearly define the family of hypotheses and the error rate being controlled.

A related issue is the use of simulated null p-values by repeatedly sampling from P. In the open-weight setting this is feasible, but for API drift detection over time or closed-model auditing, the reference distribution may itself only be available through finite samples. The permutation alternative is mentioned, but the paper says it may reduce power and relegates details to the appendix. Since one of the paper’s selling points is practical auditing by users, I would like a more central treatment of the finite-reference regime. In many realistic settings, the user will not have cheap resampling access to P, or P itself may be noisy due to API nondeterminism and temporal drift. How robust is the method then?

Third, while the Hamming kernel is empirically effective, the paper does not fully characterize when it should or should not work. Since it is only a pseudometric, there are nontrivial alternatives it cannot distinguish. The paper notes this, but the practical implications are underexplored. For example, if two models differ mainly in semantic preferences while preserving local token overlap, or differ through paraphrastic variation that is not well captured by position-wise character/token matches, Hamming MMD may have low power. The weak performance on fp16 versus fp32 is one hint. I would have liked either a more principled discussion of the alternatives to which Hamming MMD is sensitive, or additional experiments with semantically informed kernels or embedding-based kernels. As it stands, the paper’s main recommendation is empirically motivated but somewhat narrow.

The prompt distribution used in simulation also raises questions about external validity. The main synthetic evaluation uses 25 random 100-character Wikipedia prefixes across several languages, with temperature 1 and length 50. This is a reasonable stress test for long-form continuation, but it is not obviously representative of many API use cases, especially instruction following, chat, tool use, or code generation. The paper partially addresses this in the API audit by adding HumanEval and UltraChat for smaller models, which is good, but the core kernel-selection result is still mostly based on the Wikipedia continuation setup. I would be more convinced if the kernel comparison itself were repeated on at least one instruction-following and one coding distribution, since the relative advantage of Hamming versus other tests may depend strongly on task structure.

I also think the baseline set could be stronger. The paper compares against one-hot MMD, all-substrings MMD, and two multinomial tests. These are reasonable but somewhat limited. Since the central challenge is testing equality in a structured high-dimensional output space, stronger baselines might include n-gram kernels, edit-distance kernels, embedding-based kernels over completions, classifier two-sample tests, or tests based on summary statistics of token distributions if logprobs are available. Even if some of these are more expensive or require extra access, including one or two stronger alternatives would better establish that Hamming is not just beating strawman exact-match methods. In particular, a learned or pretrained embedding kernel over text might be a serious competitor in the low-sample regime.

Another concern is the dependence of the test on exact decoding parameter matching. The paper states that P and Q operate with the same decoding parameters, but in practice APIs may not implement temperature identically, may clip or renormalize logits differently, or may silently ignore unsupported parameters. Since one of the motivating examples is “incorrectly implement some decoding parameters,” this is not merely nuisance variation but part of the target. However, then the reference side should perhaps include sensitivity analyses over decoding settings. For example, how much MMD is induced by small temperature mismatches alone? Could some flagged endpoints simply reflect slight differences in temperature calibration rather than more substantive model changes? A controlled experiment varying temperature, top-p, repetition penalty, and stop conditions on the same model would help contextualize the effect sizes reported for providers.

The interpretation of MMD magnitudes also needs more care. The paper uses estimated Hamming MMD as an effect size and compares provider deviations to distances between entirely different models. This is intuitively appealing, but because the Hamming MMD depends on prompt distribution, output length, representation space, and kernel scaling, the absolute numbers are not directly portable across settings. The comparison “this provider is as far from the reference as GPT-3.5 is from Llama-3 8B” is striking, but it risks sounding more universal than it is. I would suggest emphasizing that these are task- and kernel-dependent relative comparisons, not intrinsic model distances.

On the positive side, I appreciated the attempt to correlate MMD with HumanEval accuracy differences. The moderate correlation is informative and supports the claim that MMD captures meaningful behavioral differences beyond benchmark scores. At the same time, the paper should avoid implying that larger MMD necessarily means worse quality. A provider could intentionally alter the distribution in ways that improve some tasks. The method detects difference, not degradation. This distinction is mostly present in the paper but should be stated more prominently, especially given the normative framing around “faithfulness.”

There are also some methodological details that need clarification. First, the notation and estimator definition should be checked carefully. Equation (4) appears to use sums over z,z' in the same dataset with normalization N(N-1), but it is not explicit whether diagonal terms are excluded; for the unbiased MMD estimator they should be. Second, the kernel is described as unit-norm, but the Hamming kernel as defined is not normalized to [0,1]; some discussion of scaling would help, especially when comparing across lengths or character versus token space. Third, when moving to character space, the effective sequence length varies substantially across models and prompts. How are shorter completions padded, and how sensitive are results to Unicode normalization and whitespace/tokenization artifacts? Fourth, the paper should report confidence intervals more systematically for power estimates and audit rejection rates, not just standard errors in some figures.

The API audit itself is interesting but would benefit from stronger controls and more transparency. Since providers may wrap prompts differently for chat/instruct models, it is important to know exactly what raw API payloads were sent, whether chat templates were standardized, whether system prompts were empty, and whether providers inserted hidden preambles. Similarly, were stop sequences disabled consistently? Were max token limits always honored? Were retries or rate limits handled in a way that could bias samples? Because the headline empirical result is likely to attract attention, reproducibility and procedural detail matter a lot here.

I also wonder about temporal confounding. If reference samples from Hugging Face models and API samples were collected at different times, and if providers updated endpoints during collection, then some observed differences may reflect time variation rather than stable endpoint behavior. The paper mentions dates in the appendix, but the main text should summarize the collection window and whether repeated audits over time were stable. Since one of the motivating applications is drift detection, it would be valuable to include at least one longitudinal case study showing the method detecting a known or suspected endpoint change over time.

The finetuning experiment is suggestive but somewhat limited. Finetuning on 1000 examples with a small learning rate and detecting changes after one epoch is interesting, but it would help to quantify the actual behavioral magnitude of those changes beyond power curves. For example, how large is the estimated MMD relative to quantization or watermarking? Does the test detect LoRA finetuning as well as full finetuning? Since many practical provider modifications are lightweight adapters rather than full finetunes, this would improve relevance.

In terms of writing, the paper is generally clear and readable, but there are many typographical and grammatical issues throughout the provided text. Examples include “watermarkd,” “differnt,” “machinary,” “generelly,” “sensitives,” “then recent,” and several subject-verb agreement problems. These do not obscure the main ideas, but for a top-tier venue the manuscript should be carefully proofread. Some claims could also be phrased more cautiously to avoid overstatement.

I think the paper would be significantly strengthened by the following additions or revisions. First, provide a clearer statistical treatment of the endpoint-level decision rule used in the API audit, including either a proof or simulation-based calibration of the effective false positive rate under repeated testing and thresholding. Second, broaden the kernel comparison to at least one instruction-following and one coding task, and ideally include one stronger semantic baseline such as an embedding kernel or classifier two-sample test. Third, add controlled ablations showing the MMD induced by decoding mismatches alone, such as temperature or top-p perturbations, to contextualize provider deviations. Fourth, sharpen the claims about what the method identifies: observable distributional differences under a query protocol, not necessarily weight-level modifications. Fifth, improve reproducibility details for the API experiments and summarize them in the main paper rather than only the appendix.

Despite these concerns, I view the paper as a meaningful contribution. The problem is important, the formulation is elegant, and the empirical results are provocative in a way that will likely matter to both researchers and practitioners. The work opens a useful line of inquiry at the intersection of statistical testing and LLM systems auditing. My overall assessment is positive, though not without reservations. The main reasons are the novelty and practical significance of the problem formulation, the simplicity and effectiveness of the proposed test, and the real-world API audit. The main reasons for caution are the somewhat heuristic statistical procedure in the audit, limited baseline breadth, and the need for more careful interpretation of what a rejection means.

If I were making a recommendation, I would lean toward acceptance provided the authors address the statistical calibration and claim-scope issues convincingly in revision.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper formulates auditing black-box LLM APIs as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, termed Model Equality Testing, where one compares samples from an API distribution against samples from a reference model or earlier API snapshot. The main proposal is to use MMD-based two-sample tests with string kernels, especially a simple Hamming kernel over completions, to detect distributional distortions such as quantization, watermarking, finetuning, or model substitution. Through simulations on long-form generation tasks, the authors report that the Hamming-MMD test has substantially better power than one-hot, substring, and multinomial baselines in low-sample regimes. They then apply the method to 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama-family models and report that 11 endpoints appear statistically different from Meta reference weights. The paper also uses estimated MMD values as a notion of effect size / similarity between models and providers.
strengths: Timely and practically important problem: black-box API auditing for LLMs is increasingly relevant for reproducibility, benchmarking, and user trust.
Clear formalization of API auditing as a two-sample testing problem, which unifies several use cases such as provider fidelity and temporal drift.
Method is conceptually simple and broadly applicable: it only requires sample access and does not rely on log-probabilities or provider cooperation.
Empirical study is fairly extensive, covering multiple distortions (quantization, watermarking, finetuning, model swaps), multiple models, and real commercial APIs.
The Hamming-kernel MMD choice is computationally simple and appears empirically effective in low-sample settings, which is important for practical auditing cost.
The paper goes beyond binary testing by also estimating pairwise distances between models/providers, which is a useful exploratory tool.
Open-sourcing code and a large completion dataset improves reproducibility and potential downstream impact.
weaknesses: The central methodological contribution is limited: the paper mainly adapts standard MMD two-sample testing with a hand-chosen kernel, and much of the novelty is in the application rather than new statistical methodology.

The proposed Hamming kernel is explicitly non-characteristic / only induces a pseudometric, so the test can systematically miss important distributional differences; the paper acknowledges this but does not characterize when this failure is likely in realistic LLM settings.

The empirical prompt distributions used for core simulations are narrow and somewhat artificial (e.g., 25 random Wikipedia prefixes), raising concerns about how well reported power generalizes to realistic user workloads.

The API audit conclusions are strong, but causal attribution is weak: a rejection only shows distributional difference, not whether the provider quantized, watermarked, changed decoding, altered stop conditions, modified tokenization, or had implementation mismatches.

The decision rule for endpoint failure is ad hoc: averaging rejection rates over ten repeated tests and declaring failure if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5 is not a standard hypothesis-testing procedure and lacks a formal error-control guarantee.

The paper does not sufficiently analyze sensitivity to uncontrolled API-side factors such as hidden system prompts, undocumented preprocessing/postprocessing, server-side truncation, safety filters, or nondeterministic decoding implementations.
Comparisons in character space across APIs may confound model differences with detokenization and formatting differences, especially for code and chat tasks.
Some claims about practical significance rely on raw MMD magnitudes, but the interpretation of absolute Hamming-MMD values is not well calibrated.
methodological_flaws: The composite-null testing procedure in Section 5 controls type-I error for a single run of the conjunction rule p1<alpha AND p2<alpha, but the actual endpoint-level decision used in experiments is different: they repeat tests ten times and classify an endpoint as failed if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5. No formal family-wise or per-endpoint false positive control is provided for this final procedure, so the statistical validity of the headline '11 out of 31 endpoints' claim is unclear.

The paper estimates p-values under the null by repeatedly sampling from the reference model P. This assumes the local reference implementation exactly represents the intended null distribution and that Monte Carlo error is negligible. But for open-weight LLMs, implementation details (sampling library, RNG, tokenizer version, stopping behavior, precision, hardware nondeterminism) can themselves induce detectable shifts. This threatens empirical validity of API-vs-reference conclusions.

The use of the Hamming kernel over padded completions can make the test highly sensitive to superficial formatting/length differences while being insensitive to semantically meaningful but position-shifted changes. This mismatch between kernel geometry and the scientific question 'is this the same model distribution?' is a substantive methodological limitation, not just a design choice.

The paper emphasizes power comparisons across kernels/tests, but there is limited evidence that all methods are equally calibrated at the target alpha in the finite-sample regimes studied. Without explicit null calibration plots or empirical type-I error tables in the main text, power comparisons may be misleading.

The claim that the Hamming MMD is a pseudometric obeying triangle inequality may be true for the induced population quantity, but the paper does not provide enough main-text justification for using estimated MMD values as interpretable distances between models/providers. Since the estimator can be noisy and kernel-dependent, conclusions such as one provider being 'further than another model family' may overstate what is statistically supported.

The prompt distribution pi is treated as fixed and user-chosen, but many conclusions are phrased broadly (e.g., an endpoint serves a different distribution). In reality, the test only certifies inequality averaged over the chosen prompt distribution. This is a scientific-logic overreach unless conclusions are explicitly restricted to the audited task distribution.

For real API audits, multiple comparisons arise across providers, models, and prompt sets. The paper mentions a Bonferroni correction in one figure, but the main endpoint-failure table and narrative do not clearly present a unified multiplicity-control strategy for all reported discoveries.

The correlation analysis between MMD and HumanEval accuracy difference is descriptive only, yet the discussion risks implying stronger practical validation than warranted. An R^2 of 0.392 is moderate at best, and low-accuracy regimes especially undermine the interpretation of MMD as a proxy for capability difference.
